title: Calgary police officer cleared in fatal 2022 Forest Lawn shooting
subtitle: Witnesses saw suspect attacking a man and then waving a knife and stick to the traffic. He later seriously injured a police dog
article: Alberta's police watchdog has absolved a Calgary police officer involved in the death of a man found to have been harming pedestrians and threatening other officers in Forest Lawn with a stick and a knife in 2022.

The incident occurred on Feb. 19, 2022, after a witness observed a man with a "strange" gait striding behind a bus station along 17 Avenue between 44 and 45 Street S.E. He was seen following a pedestrian, who walked away, according to footage recorded by cameras installed at the bus station.

Soon, the police received several 911 calls from people who complained about the suspect attacking a man and then waving a knife and stick to the traffic. It is unclear if the pedestrian, who was earlier chased, was attacked by the assailant. However, he soon approached a police officer.

In 20 minutes, five police officers flanked the suspect who was seated on a sidewalk. The report draws its conclusions from a series of developments, which were recorded via body cameras.
The officers made numerous attempts to befriend the suspect while requesting him to drop his weapon.
"We're just trying to help you, but it's hard to do it when you have a knife in your hand," said one police officer in a series of exchanges.
The suspect often made inscrutable, sometimes contradictory remarks - once, asking officers not to shoot and then following it up with a demand to kill him.

Another witness who was the suspect's friend approached the police officers and told the man had been kicked out of his home - to which officers responded by telling the suspect they could help him find a place to stay. However, the man refused to co-operate.

The encounter continued until the suspect stood up, then got down on one knee, picking up his walking stick and knife. The officers kept telling him to drop his weapons while he switched them between hands. After several failed attempts to offer help, an officer fired a less-lethal baton launcher at the suspect.
The man stood up and crouched. After seeing he refused to drop his weapon, the officer fired another round of the baton launcher. The suspect then charged at the officers.

Another officer allowed a police dog to have more leash and the canine moved toward the suspect. According to the report, the suspect didn't stop, so another officer launched a taser at the man. The man then struck the canine with the knife.

The dog bit his T-shirt, after which the suspect stabbed it again, this time almost killing the animal. The man then charged at the officer. The officer responded by firing three shots in quick succession. The man was declared dead on the scene after the EMS was called.
Doug King, criminologist at Mount Royal University, said he was impressed with the thoroughness of the report, which at times read like a novel.

"A lot of that flows from the fact there were so many different points of information," he said. "So from that perspective, I thought it was a good report, because when the episode took place, originally, there was a lot of questioning of the police in terms of, 'Did you use force too quickly?'"
"Anybody who was skeptical of the police's additional response should read the report ," he added.

"But also reading the report just struck home with me how tragic a situation this was - this individual who was eventually shot and killed was in clearly some kind of, if not mental distress, certainly emotional distress."
Analyzing the circumstances of the situation and several interviews thereafter, the report found the officers' use of force was proportional and justified.

"It was reasonable to believe that the AP was threatening to use force on the subject officers or other officers around them," the report stated. "They acted to defend themselves, and they acted reasonably."
King concurs with the conclusion, although he wonders if the presence of the police canine, which is usually brought in to intimidate the suspect, escalated the violence that ensued.
"But that's hindsight," he said.
"All in all, what a horribly tragic situation that ended in a way that I think no one at that scene wanted it to end that way."
